entries.a252398c017b22b80e3a13e87e99894c71b85ec0: <div sID="gen18638" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Ezek.14" sID="Ezek.14"/> <div eID="gen18638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18639" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18640" type="x-p"/> Hearing the word, and prayer, are two great ordinances of God, in which we are to give honour to him and may hope to find favour and acceptance with him; and yet in this chapter, to our great surprise, we find some waiting upon God in the one and some in the other and yet not meeting with success as they expected. I. The elders of Israel come to hear the word, and enquire of the prophet, but, because they are not duly qualified, they meet with a rebuke instead of acceptance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1-Ezek.14.5">ver. 1-5</reference>) and are called upon to repent of their sins and reform their lives, else it is at their peril to enquire of God, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6-Ezek.14.11">ver. 6-11</reference>. II. Noah, Daniel, and Job, are supposed to pray for this people, and yet, because the decree has gone forth, and the destruction of them is determined by a variety of judgments, their prayers shall not be answered, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.12-Ezek.14.21">ver. 12-21</reference>. And yet it is promised, in the close, that a remnant shall escape, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.22-Ezek.14.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>.
entries.ea3653bc0accd0575ba2a9ba4d0b0b2fa025f63d: <div eID="gen18640" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18639" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Elders of Israel Rebuked; The Prophet's Address to the Elders. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18641" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then came certain of the elders of Israel unto me, and sat before me. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">3</hi> Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumbling-block of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them? <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore speak unto them, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Every man of the house of Israel that setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to the prophet; I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will answer him that cometh according to the multitude of his idols; <hi type="super">5</hi> That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from me through their idols. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Repent, and turn <hi type="italic">yourselves</hi> from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations. <hi type="super">7</hi> For every one of the house of Israel, or of the stranger that sojourneth in Israel, which separateth himself from me, and setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to a prophet to enquire of him concerning me; I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will answer him by myself: <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will set my face against that man, and will make him a sign and a proverb, and I will cut him off from the midst of my people; and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they shall bear the punishment of their iniquity: the punishment of the prophet shall be even as the punishment of him that seeketh <hi type="italic">unto him;</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> That the house of Israel may go no more astray from me, neither be polluted any more with all their transgressions; but that they may be my people, and I may be their God, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18642" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The address which some of the elders of Israel made to the prophet, as an oracle, to enquire of the Lord by him. They <hi type="italic">came, and sat before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1">v. 1</reference>. It is probable that they were not of those who were now his fellow-captives, and constantly attended his ministry (such as those we read of <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">ch. viii. 1</reference>), but some occasional hearers, some of the grandees of Jerusalem who had come upon business to Babylon, perhaps public business, on an embassy from the king, and in their way called on the prophet, having heard much of him and being desirous to know if he had any message from God, which might be some guide to them in their negotiation. By the severe answer given them one would suspect they had a design to ensnare the prophet, or to try if they could catch hold of any thing that might look like a contradiction to Jeremiah's prophecies, and so they might have occasion to reproach them both. However, they feigned themselves just men, complimented the prophet, and sat before him gravely enough, as God's people used to sit. Note, It is no new thing for bad men to be found employed in the external performances of religion. <div eID="gen18642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18643" type="x-p"/> II. The account which God gave the prophet privately concerning them. They were strangers to him; he only knew that they were <hi type="italic">elders of Israel;</hi> that was the character they wore, and as such he received them with respect, and, it is likely, was glad to see them so well disposed. But God gives him their real character (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">v. 3</reference>); they were idolaters, and did only consult Ezekiel as they would any oracle of a pretended deity, to gratify their curiosity, and therefore he appeals to the prophet himself whether they deserved to have any countenance or encouragement given them: "<hi type="italic">Should I be enquired of at all by them?</hi> Should I accept their enquiries as an honour to myself, or answer them for satisfaction to them? No; they have no reason to expect it;" for, 1. They <hi type="italic">have set up their idols in their heart;</hi> they not only have idols, but they are in love with them, they dote upon them, are wedded to them, and have laid them so near their hearts, and have given them so great a room in their affections, that there is no parting with them. The idols they have set up in their houses, though they are now at a distance from <hi type="italic">the chambers of their imagery,</hi> yet they have them in their hearts, and they are ever and anon worshipping them in their fancies and imaginations. <hi type="italic">They have made their idols to ascend upon their hearts</hi> (so the word is); they have subjected their hearts to their idols, they are upon the throne there. Or when they came to enquire of the prophet they pretended to put away their idols, but it was in pretence only; they still had a secret reserve for them. They kept them <hi type="italic">up in their hearts;</hi> and, if they left them for a while, it was <hi type="italic">cum animo revertendi—with an intention to return to them,</hi> not a final farewell. Or it may be understood of spiritual idolatry; those whose affections are placed upon the wealth of the world and the pleasures of sense, whose god is their money, <hi type="italic">whose god is their belly,</hi> they <hi type="italic">set up their idols in their heart.</hi> Many who have no idols in their sanctuary have idols in their hearts, which is no less a usurpation of God's throne and a profanation of his name. <hi type="italic">Little children, keep yourselves from</hi> those <hi type="italic">idols.</hi> 2. They <hi type="italic">put the stumbling-block of their iniquity before their face.</hi> Their <hi type="italic">silver and gold</hi> were called <hi type="italic">the stumbling-block of their iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">ch. vii. 19</reference>), their <hi type="italic">idols of silver and gold,</hi> by the beauty of which they were allured to idolatry, and so it was the block at which they stumbled, and fell into that sin; or <hi type="italic">their iniquity</hi> is their <hi type="italic">stumbling-block,</hi> which throws them down, so that they fall into ruin. Note, Sinners are their own tempters (<hi type="italic">every man is tempted when he is drawn aside of his own lust</hi>), and so they are their own destroyers. <hi type="italic">If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it;</hi> and thus <hi type="italic">they put the stumbling-block of their iniquity before their</hi> own <hi type="italic">faces,</hi> and stumble upon it though they see it before their eyes. It intimates that they are resolved to go on in sin, whatever comes of it. <hi type="italic">I have loved strangers, and after them I will go;</hi> that is the language of their hearts. And <hi type="italic">should</hi> God <hi type="italic">be enquired of</hi> by such wretches? Do they not hereby rather put an affront upon him than do him any honour, as those did who <hi type="italic">bowed the knee</hi> to Christ in mockery? Can those expect an answer of peace from God who thus continue their acts of hostility against him? "Ezekiel, what thinkest thou of it?" <div eID="gen18643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18644" type="x-p"/> III. The answer which God, in just displeasure, orders Ezekiel to give them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">v. 4</reference>. Let them know that it is not out of any disrespect to their persons that God refuses to give them an answer, but it is laid down as a rule for <hi type="italic">every man of the house of Israel,</hi> whoever he be, that if he continue in love and league with his idols, and come to enquire of God, God will resent it as an indignity done to him, and will answer him according to his real iniquity, not according to his pretended piety. He <hi type="italic">comes to the prophet,</hi> who, he expects, will be civil to him, but God will give him his answer, by punishing him for his impudence: <hi type="italic">I the Lord,</hi> who <hi type="italic">speak and it is done, I will answer him that cometh, according to the multitude of his idols.</hi> Observe, Those who <hi type="italic">set up idols in their hearts,</hi> and set their hearts upon their idols, commonly have a multitude of them. Humble worshippers God answers <hi type="italic">according to the multitude of his mercies,</hi> but bold intruders he answers <hi type="italic">according to the multitude of their idols,</hi> that is, 1. According to the desire of their idols; he will give them up <hi type="italic">to their own hearts' lust,</hi> and leave them to themselves to be as bad as they have a mind to be, till they <hi type="italic">have filled up the measure of their iniquity.</hi> Men's corruptions are <hi type="italic">idols in their hearts,</hi> and they are of their own setting up; their temptations are <hi type="italic">the stumbling-block of their iniquity,</hi> and they are of their own putting, and God will answer them accordingly; let them take their course. 2. According to the desert of their idols; they shall have such an answer as it is just that such idolaters should have. God will punish them as he usually punishes idolaters, that is, when they stand in need of his help he will <hi type="italic">send them to the gods whom they have chosen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.13-Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 13, 14</reference>. Note, The judgment of God will dwell with men according to what they are really (that is, according to what their hearts are), not according to what they are in show and profession. And what will be the end of this? What will this threatened answer amount to? He tells them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart,</hi> may lay them open to the world, that they may be ashamed; nay, lay them open to the curse, that they may be ruined. Note, The sin and shame, and pain and ruin, of sinners, are all from themselves, and their own hearts are the snares in which they are taken; they seduce them, they betray them; their own consciences witness against them, condemn them, and are a terror to them. If God take them, if he discover them, if he convict them, if he bind them over to his judgment, it is all by <hi type="italic">their own hearts. O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself. The house of Israel</hi> is ruined by its own hands, <hi type="italic">because they are all estranged from me through their idols.</hi> Note, (1.) The ruin of sinners is owing to their estrangement from God. (2.) It is through some idol or other that the hearts of men are estranged from God; some creature has gained that place and dominion in the heart that God should have. <div eID="gen18644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18645" type="x-p"/> IV. The extent of this answer which God had given them—to all <hi type="italic">the house of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7-Ezek.14.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. The same thing is repeated, which intimates God's just displeasure against hypocrites, who mock him with the shows and forms of devotion, while their hearts are estranged from him and at war with him. Observe, 1. To whom this declaration belongs. It concerns not only every one of the house of Israel (as before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">v. 4</reference>), but <hi type="italic">the stranger that sojourns in Israel;</hi> let him not think it will be an excuse for him in his idolatries that he is but a stranger and a sojourner in Israel, and does but worship the gods that his father served and that he himself was bred up in the service of; no, let him not expect any benefit from Israel's oracles or prophets unless he thoroughly renounce his idolatry. Note, Even proselytes shall not be countenanced if they be not sincere: a dissembled conversion is no conversion. 2. The description here given of hypocrites: They <hi type="italic">separate themselves from</hi> God by their fellowship with idols; they cut themselves off from their relation to God and their interest in him; they break off their acquaintance and intercourse with him, and set themselves at a distance from him. Note, Those that join themselves to idols separate themselves from God; nor shall any be for ever separated from the vision and fruition of God, but such as now separate themselves from his service and wilfully withdraw their allegiance from him. But there are those who thus separate themselves from God, and yet come to the prophets with a seeming respect and deference to their office, <hi type="italic">to enquire of them concerning</hi> God, in order to satisfy a vain curiosity, to stop the mouth of a clamorous conscience, or to get or save a reputation among men, but without any desire to be acquainted with God or any design to be ruled by him. 3. The doom of those who thus trifle with God and think to impose upon him: "<hi type="italic">I the Lord will answer him by myself;</hi> let me alone to deal with him; I will give him an answer that shall fill him with confusion, that shall make him repent of his daring impiety." He shall have his answer, not by the words of the prophet, but by the judgments of God. <hi type="italic">And I will set my face against that man,</hi> which denotes great displeasure against him and a fixed resolution to ruin him. God can outface the most impenitent sinner. The hypocrite thought to save his credit, nay, and to gain applause, but, on the contrary, God <hi type="italic">will make him a sign and a proverb,</hi> will inflict such judgments upon him as shall make him remarkable and contemptible in the eyes of all about him; his misery shall be made use of to express the greatest misery, as when the worst of sinners are said to have <hi type="italic">their portion appointed them with hypocrites,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">Matt. xxiv. 51</reference>. God will make him an example; his judgments upon him shall be for warning to others to take heed of mocking God: for <hi type="italic">thus shall it be done to the man that separates himself from</hi> God, and yet pretends to <hi type="italic">enquire concerning him.</hi> The hypocrite thought to pass for one of God's people, and to crowd into heaven among them; but God <hi type="italic">will cut him off from the midst of his people,</hi> will discover him, and pluck him out from the thickest of them; and by this, says God, <hi type="italic">you shall know that I am the Lord.</hi> By the discovery of hypocrites it appears that God is omniscient: ministers know not how people stand affected when they come to hear the word, but God does. And by the punishment of hypocrites it appears that he is a jealous God, and one that cannot and will not be imposed upon. <div eID="gen18645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18646" type="x-p"/> V. The doom of those pretenders to prophecy who give countenance to these pretenders to piety, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9-Ezek.14.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. These hypocritical enquirers, though Ezekiel will not give them a comfortable answer, yet hope to meet with some other prophets that will; and if they do, as perhaps they may, let them know that God permits those lying prophets to deceive them in part of punishment: "<hi type="italic">If the prophet</hi> that flatters them <hi type="italic">be deceived,</hi> and gives them hopes which there is no ground for, <hi type="italic">I the Lord have deceived that prophet,</hi> have suffered the temptation to be laid before him, and suffered him to yield to it, and overruled it for the hardening of those in their wicked courses who were resolved to go on in them." We are sure that God is not the author of sin, but we are sure that he is the Lord of all and the Judge of sinners, and that he often makes use of one wicked man to destroy another, and so of one wicked man to deceive another. Both are sins in him who does them, and so they are <hi type="italic">not</hi> from God; both are punishments to him to whom they are done, and so they <hi type="italic">are</hi> from God. We have a full instance of this in the story of Ahab's prophets, who were deceived by a lying spirit, which God put into their mouths (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">1 Kings xxii. 23</reference>), and another in those whom God <hi type="italic">gives up to strong delusions, to believe a lie, because they received not the love of the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.11">2 Thess. ii. 10, 11</reference>. But read the fearful doom of the lying prophet: <hi type="italic">I will stretch out my hand upon him and will destroy him.</hi> When God has served his own righteous purposes by him he shall be reckoned with for his unrighteous purposes. As, when God had made use of the Chaldeans for the wasting of a sinful people, he justly punished them for their rage, so when he had made use of <hi type="italic">false prophets,</hi> and afterwards of <hi type="italic">false Christs,</hi> for the deceiving of a sinful people, he justly punished them for their falsehood. But herein we must acknowledge (as Calvin upon this place reminds us) that God's <hi type="italic">judgments are a great deep,</hi> that we are incompetent judges of them, and that, though we cannot account for the equity of God's proceedings to the satisfying and silencing of every caviller, yet there is a day coming when he will be justified before all the world, and particularly in this instance, when <hi type="italic">the punishment of the prophet</hi> that flattereth the hypocrite in his evil way shall be as the punishment of the hypocrite that seeketh to him and bespeaks <hi type="italic">smooth things</hi> only, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. The ditch shall be the same to the blind leader and the blind followers. <div eID="gen18646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18647" type="x-p"/> VI. The good counsel that is given them for the preventing of this fearful doom (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Therefore repent, and turn yourselves from your idols.</hi> Let <hi type="italic">this</hi> separate between you and them, that they separate between you and God; because they set God's face against you, do you <hi type="italic">turn away your faces from them,</hi>" which denotes, not only forsaking them, but forsaking them with loathing and detestation: "Turn from them as from abominations that you are sick of; and then you will be welcome to enquire of the Lord. <hi type="italic">Come now, and let us reason together.</hi>" <div eID="gen18647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18648" type="x-p"/> VII. The good issue of all this as to the house of Israel; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the pretending prophets, and the pretending saints, shall perish together by the judgments of God, that, some being made examples, the body of the people may be reformed, <hi type="italic">that the house of Israel may go no more astray from me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, The punishments of some are designed for the prevention of sin, that others may hear, and fear, and take warning. When we see what becomes of those that go astray from God we should thereby be engaged to keep close to him. And, if <hi type="italic">the house of Israel go not astray, they will not be polluted any more.</hi> Note, Sin is a polluting thing; it renders the sinner odious in the eyes of the pure and holy God, and in his own eyes too whenever conscience is awakened; and therefore they shall <hi type="italic">no more be polluted, that they may be my people and I may be their God.</hi> Note, Those whom God takes into covenant with himself must first be cleansed from the pollutions of sin; and those who are so cleansed shall not only be saved from ruin, but be entitled to all the privileges of God's people.
entries.2b3d3820c8c9d19e50b661fdf3843d874bbb5c79: <div eID="gen18648" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction of the People Determined; The Variety of the Divine Judgment; A Remnant Preserved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  593.)</title> <div sID="gen18649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came again to me, saying, <hi type="super">13</hi> Son of man, when the land sinneth against me by trespassing grievously, then will I stretch out mine hand upon it, and will break the staff of the bread thereof, and will send famine upon it, and will cut off man and beast from it: <hi type="super">14</hi> Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver <hi type="italic">but</hi> their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land, and they spoil it, so that it be desolate, that no man may pass through because of the beasts:   16 <hi type="italic">Though</hi> these three men <hi type="italic">were</hi> in it, <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters; they only shall be delivered, but the land shall be desolate. <hi type="super">17</hi> Or <hi type="italic">if</hi> I bring a sword upon that land, and say, Sword, go through the land; so that I cut off man and beast from it: <hi type="super">18</hi> Though these three men <hi type="italic">were</hi> in it, <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they only shall be delivered themselves. <hi type="super">19</hi> Or <hi type="italic">if</hi> I send a pestilence into that land, and pour out my fury upon it in blood, to cut off from it man and beast: <hi type="super">20</hi> Though Noah, Daniel, and Job, <hi type="italic">were</hi> in it, <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , they shall deliver neither son nor daughter; they shall <hi type="italic">but</hi> deliver their own souls by their righteousness. <hi type="super">21</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; How much more when I send my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast? <hi type="super">22</hi> Yet, behold, therein shall be left a remnant that shall be brought forth, <hi type="italic">both</hi> sons and daughters: behold, they shall come forth unto you, and ye shall see their way and their doings: and ye shall be comforted concerning the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">even</hi> concerning all that I have brought upon it. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they shall comfort you, when ye see their ways and their doings: and ye shall know that I have not done without cause all that I have done in it, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18650" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to show, <div eID="gen18650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18651" type="x-p"/> I. That national sins bring national judgments. When virtue is ruined and laid waste every thing else will soon be ruined and laid waste too (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">When the land sins against me,</hi> when vice and wickedness become epidemical, <hi type="italic">when the land sins by trespassing grievously,</hi> when the sinners have become very numerous and their sins very heinous, when gross impieties and immoralities universally prevail, <hi type="italic">then will I stretch forth my hand upon it,</hi> for the punishment of it. The divine power shall be vigorously and openly exerted; the judgments shall be extended and stretched forth to all the corners of the land, to all the concerns and interests of the nation. Grievous sins bring grievous plagues. <div eID="gen18651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18652" type="x-p"/> II. That God has a variety of sore judgments wherewith to punish sinful nations, and he has them all at command and inflicts which he pleases. He did indeed give David his choice what judgment he would be punished with for his sin in numbering the people; for any of them would serve to answer the end, which was to lessen the numbers he was proud of; but David, in effect, referred it to God again: "<hi type="italic">Let us fall into the hands of the Lord;</hi> let him choose with what rod we shall be beaten." But he uses a variety of judgments that it may appear he has a universal dominion, and that in all our concerns we may see our dependence on him. <hi type="italic">Four sore judgments</hi> are here specified:— 1. <hi type="italic">Famine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.13">v. 13</reference>. The denying and withholding of common mercies is itself judgment enough, there needs no more to make a people miserable. God needs not bring the staff of oppression, it is but <hi type="italic">breaking the staff of bread</hi> and the work is soon done; he <hi type="italic">cuts off man and beast</hi> by cutting off the provisions which nature makes for both in the annual products of the earth. God <hi type="italic">breaks the staff of bread</hi> when, though we have bread, yet we are not nourished and strengthened by it. <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">You eat, but you have not enough.</hi> 2. Hurtful <hi type="italic">beasts, noisome</hi> and noxious, either as poisonous or as ravenous. God can make these <hi type="italic">to pass through the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.15">v. 15</reference>), to increase in all parts of it, and to bereave it, not only of the tame cattle, preying upon their flocks and herds, but of their people, devouring men, women, and children, so <hi type="italic">that no man may pass through because of the beasts;</hi> none dare travel even in the high roads for fear of being pulled in pieces by lions, or other beasts of prey, as the children of Beth-el by two bears. Note, When men revolt from their allegiance to God, and rebel against him, it is just with God that the inferior creatures should rise up in arms against men, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.22">Lev. xxvi. 22</reference>. 3. War. God often chastises sinful nations by bringing a sword upon them, the sword of a foreign enemy, and he gives it its commission and orders what execution it shall do (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.17">v. 17</reference>): he says, <hi type="italic">Sword, go through the land.</hi> It is bad enough if the sword do but enter into the borders of a land, but much worse when it goes through the bowels of a land. By it God <hi type="italic">cuts off man and beast,</hi> horse and foot. What execution the sword does God does by it; for it is his sword, and it acts as he directs. 4. <hi type="italic">Pestilence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.19">v. 19</reference>), a dreadful disease, which has sometimes depopulated cities; by it God <hi type="italic">pours out his fury in blood</hi> (that is, in death); the pestilence kills as effectually as if the blood were shed by the sword, for it is poisoned by the disease, <hi type="italic">the sickness</hi> we call it. See how miserable the case of mankind is that lies thus exposed to deaths in various shapes. See how dangerous the case of sinners is against whom God has so many ways of fighting, so that, though they escape one judgment, God has another waiting for them. <div eID="gen18652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18653" type="x-p"/> III. That when God's professing people revolt from him, and rebel against him, they may justly expect a complication of judgments to fall upon them. God has various ways of contending with a sinful nation; but if Jerusalem, the holy city, <hi type="italic">become a harlot,</hi> God will send upon her all his <hi type="italic">four sore judgments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">v. 21</reference>); for the nearer any are to God in name and profession the more severely will he reckon with them if they reproach that worthy name by which they are called and give the lie to that profession. They shall be punished <hi type="italic">seven times more.</hi> <div eID="gen18653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18654" type="x-p"/> IV. That there may be, and commonly are, some few very good men, even in those places that by sin are ripened for ruin. It is no foreign supposition that, even in a land that has <hi type="italic">trespassed grievously,</hi> there may be <hi type="italic">three</hi> such <hi type="italic">men</hi> as <hi type="italic">Noah, Daniel, and Job.</hi> Daniel was now living, and at this time had scarcely arrived at the prime of his eminency, but he was already famous (at least this word of God concerning him would without fail make him so); yet he was carried away into captivity with the first of all, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.6">Dan. i. 6</reference>. Some of the better sort of people in Jerusalem might perhaps think that, if Daniel (of whose fame in the king of Babylon's court they had heard much) had but continued in Jerusalem, it would have been spared for his sake, as the magicians in Babylon were. "No," says God, "though you had him, who was as eminently good in bad times and places as Noah in the old world and Job in the land of Uz, yet a reprieve should not be obtained." In the places that are most corrupt, and in the ages that are most degenerate, <hi type="italic">there is a remnant</hi> which God reserves to himself, and which <hi type="italic">still hold fast their integrity</hi> and stand fair for the honour of <hi type="italic">delivering the land,</hi> as <hi type="italic">the innocent</hi> are said to do, <reference osisRef="Job.22.30">Job xxii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen18654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18655" type="x-p"/> V. That God often spares very wicked places for the sake of a few godly people in them. This is implied here as the expectation of Jerusalem's friends in the day of its distress: "Surely God will stay his controversy with us; for are there not some among us that are emptying the measure of national guilt by their prayers, as others are filling it by their sins? And, rather than God will <hi type="italic">destroy the righteous with the wicked,</hi> he will preserve <hi type="italic">the wicked with the righteous.</hi> If Sodom might have been spared for the sake of ten good men, surely Jerusalem may." <div eID="gen18655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18656" type="x-p"/> VI. That such men as Noah, Daniel, and Job, will prevail, if any can, to turn away the wrath of God from a sinful people. Noah was a perfect man, and kept his integrity when all flesh had corrupted their way; and, for his sake, his family, though one of them was wicked (Ham), was saved in the ark. Job was a great example of piety, and mighty in prayer for his children, for his friends; and God turned his captivity when he prayed. Those were very ancient examples, before Moses, that great intercessor; and therefore God mentions them, to intimate that he had some very peculiar favourites long before the Jewish nation was formed or founded, and would have such when it was ruined, for which reason, it should seem, those names were made use of, rather than Moses, Aaron, or Samuel; and yet, lest any should think that God was partial in his respects to the ancient days, here is a modern instance, a living one, placed between those two that were the glories of antiquity, and he now a captive, and that is Daniel, to teach us not to lessen the useful good men of our own day by over-magnifying the ancients. Let the children of the captivity know that Daniel, their neighbour, and <hi type="italic">companion in tribulation,</hi> being a man of great humility, piety, and zeal for God, and instant and constant in prayer, had as good an interest in heaven as Noah or Job had. Why may not God raise up as great and good men now as he did formerly, and do as much for them? <div eID="gen18656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18657" type="x-p"/> VII. That when the sin of a people has come to its height, and the decree has gone forth for their ruin, the piety and prayers of the best men shall not prevail to finish the controversy. This is here asserted again and again, that, <hi type="italic">though these three men were in</hi> Jerusalem at this time, yet they should <hi type="italic">deliver neither son nor daughter;</hi> not so much as the little ones should be spared for their sakes, as the little ones of Israel were upon the prayer of Moses, <reference osisRef="Num.14.31">Num. xiv. 31</reference>. No; <hi type="italic">the land shall be desolate,</hi> and God would not hear their prayers for it, though <hi type="italic">Moses and Samuel stood before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">Jer. xv. 1</reference>. Note, Abused patience will turn at last into inexorable wrath; and it should seem as if God would be more inexorable in Jerusalem's case than in another (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6">v. 6</reference>), because, besides the divine patience, they had enjoyed greater privileges than any other people, which were the aggravations of their sin. <div eID="gen18657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18658" type="x-p"/> VIII. That, though pious praying men may not prevail to deliver others, yet <hi type="italic">they shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness,</hi> so that, though they may suffer in the common calamity, yet to them the property of it is altered; it is not to them what it is to the wicked; it is unstrung, and does them no hurt; it is sanctified, and does them good. Sometimes <hi type="italic">their souls</hi> (their lives) are remarkably <hi type="italic">delivered,</hi> and <hi type="italic">given them for a prey;</hi> at least <hi type="italic">their souls</hi> (their spiritual interests) are secured. If their bodies be not <hi type="italic">delivered,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">their souls</hi> are. <hi type="italic">Riches</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">profit not in the day of wrath,</hi> but <hi type="italic">righteousness delivers from death,</hi> from so great a death, so many deaths as are here threatened. This should encourage us to keep our integrity in times of common apostasy, that, if we do so, we shall be <hi type="italic">hidden in the day of the Lord's anger.</hi> <div eID="gen18658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18659" type="x-p"/> IX. That, even when God makes the greatest desolations by his judgments, he reserves some to be the monuments of his mercy, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.22-Ezek.14.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. In Jerusalem itself, though marked for utter ruin, yet <hi type="italic">there shall be left a remnant,</hi> who shall not be cut off by any of those <hi type="italic">sore judgments</hi> before mentioned, but shall be carried into captivity, both <hi type="italic">sons and daughters,</hi> who shall be the seed of a new generation. The young ones, who had not grown up to such an obstinacy in sin as their fathers had who were therefore cut off as incurable, these <hi type="italic">shall be brought forth</hi> out of the ruins of Jerusalem by the victorious enemy, and <hi type="italic">behold they shall come forth to you</hi> that are in captivity, they shall make a virtue of a necessity, and shall come the more willingly to Babylon because so many of their friends have gone thither before them and are there ready to receive them; and, when they come, <hi type="italic">you shall see their ways and their doing;</hi> you shall hear them make a free and ingenuous confession of the sins they had formerly been guilty of, and a humble profession of repentance for them, with promises of reformation; and you shall see instances of their reformation, shall see what good their affliction has done them, and how prudently and patiently they conduct themselves under it. Their narrow escape shall have a good effect upon them; it shall change their temper and conversation, and make them new men. And this will redound, 1. To the satisfaction of their brethren: <hi type="italic">They shall comfort you when you see their ways.</hi> Note, It is a very comfortable sight to see people, when they are under the rod, repenting and humbling themselves, justifying God and accepting the punishment of their iniquity. When we sorrow (as we ought to do) for the afflictions of others, it is a great comfort to us in our sorrow to see them improving their afflictions and making a good use of them. When those captives told their friends how bad they had been, and how righteous God was in bringing these judgments upon them, it made them very easy, and helped to reconcile them to the calamities of Jerusalem, to the justice of God in punishing his own people so, and to the goodness of God, which now appeared to have had kind intentions in all; and thus "<hi type="italic">You shall be comforted concerning all the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem,</hi> and, when you better understand the thing, shall not have such direful apprehensions concerning it as you have had." Note, It is a debt we owe to our brethren, if we have got good by our afflictions, to comfort them by letting them know it. 2. It will redound to the honour of God: "<hi type="italic">You shall know that I have not done without cause,</hi> not without a just provocation, and yet not without a gracious design, <hi type="italic">all that I have done in it.</hi>" Note, When afflictions have done their work, and have accomplished that for which they were sent, then will appear the wisdom and goodness of God in sending them, and God will be not only justified, but glorified in them.  <chapter eID="Ezek.14"/> <div eID="gen18659" type="x-p"/>

entries.ae0134b2a0bd887e34d02963b6cc1dd2c198d4e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11180"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1-Ezek.14.23">Eze 14:1-23</reference>. Hypocritical Inquirers Are Answered According to Their Hypocrisy. The Calamities Coming on the People; but a Remnant Is to Escape.</title> <div sID="gen20167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11180"/><hi type="bold">1. elders--</hi>persons holding that dignity among the exiles at the Chebar. Grotius refers this to Seraiah and those sent with him from Judea (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jr 51:59</reference>). The prophet's reply, first, reflecting on the character of the inquirers, and, secondly, foretelling the calamities coming on Judea, may furnish an idea of the subject of their inquiry.<div eID="gen20167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat before me--</hi>not at once able to find a beginning of their speech; indicative of anxiety and despondency. <div eID="gen20168" type="x-p"/>
entries.f824987d6528666f879469936238542e09d94871: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11181"/><div sID="gen20169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11181"/><hi type="bold">3. heart ... face--</hi>The heart is first corrupted, and then the outward manifestation of idol-worship follows; they set their idols before their eyes. With all their pretense of consulting God now, they have not even put away their idols outwardly; implying gross contempt of God. "Set up," literally, "aloft"; implying that their idols had gained the supreme ascendancy over them.<div eID="gen20169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stumbling-block of ... iniquity--</hi>See <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21">Pr 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.23">23</reference>, "Let not them (God's laws) depart from thine eyes, then ... thy foot shall not stumble." Instead of God's law, which (by being kept before their eyes) would have saved them from stumbling, they set up their idols before their eyes, which proved a stumbling-block, causing them to stumble (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Eze 7:19</reference>).<div eID="gen20170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inquired of at all--</hi>literally, "should I with inquiry be inquired of" by such hypocrites as they are? (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.29">Pr 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">28:9</reference>). <div eID="gen20171" type="x-p"/>
entries.85e2dd145ea5ed3049a809dc4c457e7ea33a1bb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11182"/><div sID="gen20172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11182"/><hi type="bold">4. and cometh--</hi>and yet cometh, reigning himself to be a true worshipper of Jehovah.<div eID="gen20172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that cometh--</hi>so the Hebrew Margin reads. But the Hebrew text reading is, "according to it, according to the multitude of his idols"; the anticipative clause with the pronoun not being pleonastic, but increasing the emphasis of the following clause with the noun. "I will answer," literally, reflexively, "I will Myself (or for Myself) answer him."<div eID="gen20173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to ... idols--</hi>thus, "answering a fool according to his folly"; making the sinner's sin his punishment; retributive justice (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; 26:5). <div eID="gen20174" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd7dc71365c2c049e9734382a002b721e96363a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11183"/><div sID="gen20175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11183"/><hi type="bold">5. That I may take--</hi>that is, unveil and overtake with punishment the dissimulation and impiety of Israel hid in their own heart. Or, rather, "That I may punish them by answering them after their own hearts"; corresponding to "according to the multitude of his idols" (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">Eze 14:4</reference>); an instance is given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9">Eze 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>, God giving them up in wrath to their own lie.<div eID="gen20175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">idols--</hi>though pretending to "inquire" of Me, "in their hearts" they are "estranged from Me," and love "idols." <div eID="gen20176" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b2c1f46f7ca583ad5d81223d0c71e25357f23c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11184"/><div sID="gen20177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11184"/>6. Though God so threatened the people for their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:5</reference>), yet He would rather they should avert the calamity by "repentance."<div eID="gen20177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn yourselves--</hi>Calvin translates, "turn others" (namely, the stranger proselytes in the land). As ye have been the advisers of others (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7">Eze 14:7</reference>, "the stranger that sojourneth in Israel") to idolatry, so bestow at least as much pains in turning them to the truth; the surest proof of repentance. But the parallelism to <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">4</reference> favors English Version. Their sin was twofold: (1) "In their heart" or inner man; (2) "Put before their face," that is, exhibited outwardly. So their repentance is generally expressed by "repent," and is then divided into: (1) "Turn yourselves (inwardly) from your idols"; (2) "Turn away your faces (outwardly) from all your abominations." It is not likely that an exhortation to convert others should come between the two affecting themselves. <div eID="gen20178" type="x-p"/>
entries.03dd4f2856866e63c376f3aa6ae0d39100a444c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11185"/><div sID="gen20179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11185"/><hi type="bold">7. stranger--</hi>the proselyte, tolerated in Israel only on condition of worshipping no God but Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.8">Le 17:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.17.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen20179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inquire of him concerning me--</hi>that is, concerning My will.<div eID="gen20180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by myself--</hi>not by word, but by deed, that is, by judgments, marking My hand and direct agency; instead of answering him through the prophet he consults. Fairbairn translates, as it is the same Hebrew as in the previous clause, "concerning Me," it is natural that God should use the same expression in His reply as was used in the consultation of Him. But the sense, I think, is the same. The hypocrite inquires of the prophet concerning God; and God, instead of replying through the prophet, replies for Himself concerning Himself. <div eID="gen20181" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f45ae0af26668fb1ce70c3d0f8c6273db932eb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11186"/><div sID="gen20182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11186"/><hi type="bold">8. And I will set my face against that man--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Le 17:10</reference>).<div eID="gen20182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and will make him a sign--</hi>literally, "I will destroy him so as to become a sign"; it will be no ordinary destruction, but such as will make him be an object pointed at with wonder by all, as Korah, &c. (<reference osisRef="Num.26.10">Nu 26:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">De 28:37</reference>). <div eID="gen20183" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6279167d92f26e7a4ef9a2f419cd064e3e6a937: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11187"/><div sID="gen20184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11187"/><hi type="bold">9. I the Lord have deceived that prophet--</hi>not directly, but through Satan and his ministers; not merely permissively, but by overruling their evil to serve the purposes of His righteous judgment, to be a touchstone to separate the precious from the vile, and to "prove" His people (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.3">De 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">1Ki 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.10">Jr 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). Evil comes not from God, though God overrules it to serve His will (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.3">Jas 1:3</reference>). This declaration of God is intended to answer their objection, "Jeremiah and Ezekiel are but two opposed to the many prophets who announce 'peace' to us." "Nay, deceive not yourselves, those prophets of yours are deluding you, and I permit them to do so as a righteous judgment on your wilful blindness." <div eID="gen20184" type="x-p"/>
entries.92014246f3cee4a86b6579f8d0628cdc99a945bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11188"/><div sID="gen20185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11188"/>10. As they dealt deceitfully with God by seeking answers of peace without repentance, so God would let them be dealt with deceitfully by the prophets whom they consulted. God would chastise their sin with a corresponding sin; as they rejected the safe directions of the true light, He would send the pernicious delusions of a false one; prophets would be given them who should re-echo the deceitfulness that already wrought in their own bosom, to their ruin [Fairbairn]. The people had themselves alone to blame, for they were long ago forewarned how to discern and to treat a false prophet (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.3">De 13:3</reference>); the very existence of such deceivers among them was a sign of God's judicial displeasure (compare in Saul's case, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.14">1Sa 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">28:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">7</reference>). They and the prophet, being dupes of a common delusion, should be involved in a common ruin. <div eID="gen20185" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcae15aeb86b89f9971eeae36b7ef2abbddbaa2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11189"/><div sID="gen20186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11189"/>11. Love was the spring of God's very judgments on His people, who were incurable by any other process (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.20">Eze 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.27">37:27</reference>). <div eID="gen20186" type="x-p"/>
entries.09491f20bd2a27f31e6be543b6427e2eb0dfb960: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11190"/><div sID="gen20187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11190"/>12. The second part of the chapter: the effect which the presence of a few righteous persons was to have on the purposes of God (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.24-Gen.18.32">Ge 18:24-32</reference>). God had told Jeremiah that the guilt of Judah was too great to be pardoned even for the intercession of Moses and Samuel (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jr 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">15:1</reference>), which had prevailed formerly (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.14">Ex 32:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.13-Num.14.20">Nu 14:13-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8-1Sam.7.12">1Sa 7:8-12</reference>), implying the extraordinary heinousness of their guilt, since in ordinary cases "the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man (for others) availeth much" (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>). Ezekiel supplements Jeremiah by adding that not only those two once successful intercessors, but not even the three pre-eminently righteous men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, could stay God's judgments by their righteousness. <div eID="gen20187" type="x-p"/>
entries.95a4e5f6655ff1d8f503ac7f6cd3c504722f6589: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11191"/><div sID="gen20188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11191"/><hi type="bold">13. staff of ... bread--</hi>on which man's existence is supported as on a staff (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.16">5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">Le 26:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Is 3:1</reference>). I will send a famine. <div eID="gen20188" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b9d7403a3a6e6d46987e8310dfcfa1043f212f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11192"/><div sID="gen20189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11192"/><hi type="bold">14. Noah, Daniel ... Job--</hi>specified in particular as having been saved from overwhelming calamities for their personal righteousness. Noah had the members of his family alone given to him, amidst the general wreck. Daniel saved from the fury of the king of Babylon the three youths (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.17">Da 2:17</reference>, 18, 48, 49). Though his prophecies mostly were later than those of Ezekiel, his fame for piety and wisdom was already established, and the events recorded in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1-Dan.2.49">Da 1:1-2:49</reference> had transpired. The Jews would naturally, in their fallen condition, pride themselves on one who reflected such glory on his nation at the heathen capital, and would build vain hopes (here set aside) on his influence in averting ruin from them. Thus the objection to the authenticity of Daniel from this passage vanishes. "Job" forms the climax (and is therefore put out of chronological order), having not even been left a son or a daughter, and having had himself to pass through an ordeal of suffering before his final deliverance, and therefore forming the most simple instance of the righteousness of God, which would save the righteous themselves alone in the nation, and that after an ordeal of suffering, but not spare even a son or daughter for their sake (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.16">Eze 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.20">18, 20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">14:11</reference>).<div eID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deliver ... souls by ... righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>); not the righteousness of works, but that of grace, a truth less clearly understood under the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen20190" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab54258dfe5f6bc8269f8ed6fdc2020c8d313430: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11193"/><div sID="gen20191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11193"/>15-21. The argument is cumulative. He first puts the case of the land sinning so as to fall under the judgment of a famine (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.13">Eze 14:13</reference>); then (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.15">Eze 14:15</reference>) "noisome beasts" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.22">Le 26:22</reference>); then "the sword"; then, worst of all, "pestilence." The three most righteous of men should deliver only themselves in these several four cases. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Eze 14:21</reference> he concentrates the whole in one mass of condemnation. If Noah, Daniel, Job, could not deliver the land, when deserving only one judgment, "how much more" when all four judgments combined are justly to visit the land for sin, shall these three righteous men not deliver it. <div eID="gen20191" type="x-p"/>
entries.dce4bff8e5424def43aec02dc23710ce67b15377: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11196"/><div sID="gen20194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11196"/><hi type="bold">22. Yet ... a remnant--</hi>not of righteous persons, but some of the guilty who should "come forth" from the destruction of Jerusalem to Babylon, to lead a life of hopeless exile there. The reference here is to judgment, not mercy, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.23">Eze 14:23</reference> shows.<div eID="gen20194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall see their ... doings; and ... be comforted--</hi>Ye, the exiles at the Chebar, who now murmur at God's judgment about to be inflicted on Jerusalem as harsh, when ye shall see the wicked "ways" and character of the escaped remnant, shall acknowledge that both Jerusalem and its inhabitants deserved their fate; his recognition of the righteousness of the judgment will reconcile you to it, and so ye shall be "comforted" under it [Calvin]. Then would follow mercy to the elect remnant, though that is not referred to here, but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>. <div eID="gen20195" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fcd3776eb6cf284a62c4c6a2747c8842736b9f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11197"/><div sID="gen20196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11197"/><hi type="bold">23. they shall comfort you--</hi>not in words, but by your recognizing in their manifest guilt, that God had not been unjustly severe to them and the city. <chapter eID="Ezek.14"/>

entries.6067cee5c8804d52cf5f16a113e72ffb946e8dce: <div eID="gen31527" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31528" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31529" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31529" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31528" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31530" type="x-p"/> Here God threatens those hypocrites who pretended to worship him, while they loved and practiced idolatry, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.1-Eze.14.11">Eze 14:1-11</reference>. He declares his irreversible purpose of punishing so guilty a nation, in behalf of which no intercession of the people of God shall be of any avail. The gross idolaters of Jerusalem and Judah shall be visited with God's four sore judgments, famine, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.12-Eze.14.14">Eze 14:12-14</reference>; wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.15">Eze 14:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.16">Eze 14:16</reference>; the sword, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.17">Eze 14:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.18">Eze 14:18</reference>; and pestilence, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.19-Eze.14.21">Eze 14:19-21</reference>. A remnant shall be delivered from the wrath coming upon the whole land, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.22">Eze 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.23">Eze 14:23</reference>. <div eID="gen31530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31531" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31532" type="x-p"/> Then came certain of the elders of Israel unto me - These probably came to tempt him, or get him to say something that would embroil him with the government. They were bad men, as we shall see in the third verse.
entries.27dfc1bd6977cf1d228c795c1cedfe5242409f78: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31533" type="x-p"/> These men have set up their idols in their heart - Not only in their houses; in the streets; but they had them in their hearts. These were stumbling-blocks of iniquity; they fell over them, and broke the neck of their souls. And should God be inquired of by such miscreants as these?
entries.ed259099b5358dc58f2c60308c965cbd328ce331: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31534" type="x-p"/> According to the multitude of his idols - I will treat him as an idolater, as a flagrant idolater.
entries.58629b23475e7566db7e1021d0bdf090be6698d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31535" type="x-p"/> And cometh to a prophet - Generally supposed to mean a false prophet. <div eID="gen31535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31536" type="x-p"/> I the Lord will answer him by myself - I shall discover to him, by my own true prophet, what shall be the fruit of his ways. So, while their false prophets were assuring them of peace and prosperity, God's prophets were predicting the calamities that afterwards fell upon them. Yet they believed the false prophets in preference to the true. Ahab, about to engage with the Syrians, who had possession of Ramoth-Gilead, asked Micaiah, the prophet of the Lord, concerning the event; who told him he should lose the battle. He then inquired of Zedekiah, a false prophet, who promised him a glorious victory. Ahab believed the latter, marched against the enemy, was routed, and slain in the battle, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.10">1Kgs 22:10</reference>, etc.
entries.e0826e9c19f0a2c372bb0eba17cff0f07b2e9349: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31537" type="x-p"/> I the Lord have deceived that prophet - That is, he ran before he was sent; he willingly became the servant of Satan's illusions; and I suffered this to take place, because he and his followers refused to consult and serve me. I have often had occasion to remark that it is common in the Hebrew language to state a thing as done by the Lord which he only suffers or permits to be done; for so absolute and universal is the government of God, that the smallest occurrence cannot take place without his will or permission.
entries.1f30d3028bbaba7391fca78de0cf76dc1bb47956: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31538" type="x-p"/> The punishment of the prophet - They are both equally guilty; both have left the Lord, and both shall be equally punished.
entries.e6d5fe34f5b102969cb2548e1d979a94b1066245: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31539" type="x-p"/> By trespassing grievously - Having been frequently warned, and having refused to leave their sin, and so filled up the measure of their iniquity.
entries.37d4ff6e38ad47c9dc517fa51a7d87d8f332ba4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31540" type="x-p"/> Though - Noah, Daniel, and Job - The intercession even of the holiest of men shall not avert my judgments. Noah, though a righteous man, could not by his intercession preserve the old world from being drowned. Job, though a righteous man, could not preserve his children from being killed by the fall of their house. Daniel, though a righteous man, could not prevent the captivity of his country. Daniel must have been contemporary with Ezekiel. He was taken captive in the third year of Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan 1:1</reference>. After this Jehoiakim reigned eight years, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.36">2Kgs 23:36</reference>. And this prophecy, as appears from <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>, was uttered in the sixth year of Jehoiachin's captivity, who succeeded Jehoiakim, and reigned only three months, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.6">2Kgs 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Kgs 24:8</reference>. Therefore at this time Daniel had been Fourteen years in captivity. See Newcome. Even at this time he had gained much public celebrity. From this account we may infer that Job was as real a person as Noah or Daniel; and of their identity no man has pretended to doubt. When God, as above, has determined to punish a nation, no intercession shall avail. Personal holiness alone can prevent these evils; but the holiness of any man can only avail for himself.
entries.3332b9fcccc0f706cc34c9624561a39b43130fbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen31540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31541" type="x-p"/> My four sore judgments - Sword, war. Famine, occasioned by drought. Pestilence, epidemic diseases which sweep off a great part of the inhabitants of a land. The Noisome Beast, the multiplication of wild beasts in consequence of the general destruction of the inhabitants.
entries.aadf1f2e10e434d75d3e9f329c22fe05d8db6b1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31542" type="x-p"/> Behold, they shall come forth unto you - Though there shall be great desolations in the land of Judea, yet a remnant shall be left that shall come here also as captives; and their account of the abominations of the people shall prove to you with what propriety I have acted in abandoning them to such general destruction. This speech is addressed to those who were already in captivity; i.e., those who had been led to Babylon with their king Jeconiah.
entries.9830d758c4a2b9c223501698029abbed596be03d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen31542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31543" type="x-p"/> Ye shall know that I have not done without cause - There is no part of the conduct of God towards man that is not dictated by the purest principles of justice, equity, and truth. He does nothing but what is right; and whatever is right to be done, that ought to be done. In God's justice there is no severity; in God's mercy there is no caprice. He alone doth all things well; for he is the Fountain of justice and mercy.  <chapter eID="Ezek.14"/> <div eID="gen31543" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b3a6a6a920683d934ae1fefed969137c03cd711: <div eID="gen14892" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Attitude of God Towards the Worshippers of Idols, and Certainty of the Judgments</title> <div sID="gen14893" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains two words of God, which have obviously an internal connection with each other. The first (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1-Ezek.14.11">Eze 14:1-11</reference>) announces to the elders, who have come to the prophet to inquire of God, that the Lord will not allow idolaters to inquire of Him, but will answer all who do not turn from idolatry with severe judgments, and will even destroy the prophets who venture to give an answer to such inquirers. The second (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.12-Ezek.14.23">Eze 14:12-23</reference>) denounces the false hope that God will avert the judgment and spare Jerusalem because of the righteousness of the godly men therein. <div eID="gen14893" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lord Gives No Answer to the Idolaters</title> <div sID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1">Eze 14:1</reference> narrates the occasion for this and the following words of God: <hi type="italic">There came to me men of the elders of Israel, and sat down before me.</hi> These men were not deputies from the Israelites in Palestine, as Grotius and others suppose, but elders of the exiles among whom Ezekiel had been labouring. They came to visit the prophet (v. 3), evidently with the intention of obtaining, through him, a word of God concerning the future of Jerusalem, or the fate of the kingdom of Judah. But Hävernick is wrong in supposing that we may infer, from either the first or second word of God in this chapter, that they had addressed to the prophet a distinct inquiry of this nature, to which the answer is given in vv. 12-23. For although their coming to the prophet showed that his prophecies had made an impression upon them, it is not stated in v. 1 that they had come to inquire of God, like the elders in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>, and there is no allusion to any definite questions in the words of God themselves. The first (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.2-Ezek.14.11">Eze 14:2-11</reference>) simply assumes that they have come with the intention of asking, and discloses the state of heart which keeps them from coming to inquire; and the second (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.12-Ezek.14.23">Eze 14:12-23</reference>) points out the worthlessness of their false confidence in the righteousness of certain godly men.
entries.4194c289acad6bbc8dad031fbc4a6cb273cb0725: <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.2-Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:2-5</reference> <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 14:3. <hi type="italic">Son of man, these men have let their idols rise up in their heart, and have set the stumbling-block to guilt before their face: shall I allow myself to be inquired of by them?</hi> Eze 14:4. <hi type="italic">Therefore speak to them, and say to them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Every man of the house of Israel who lifteth up his idols in his heart, and setteth the stumbling-block to his sin before his face, and cometh to the prophet, to him do I, Jehovah, show myself, answering according thereto, according to the multitude of his idols;</hi> Eze 14:5. <hi type="italic">To grasp the house of Israel by their heart, because they have turned away from me, all of them through their idols.</hi> - We have not to picture these elders to ourselves as given up to gross idolatry. העלה על לב means, to allow anything to come into the mind, to permit it to rise up in the heart, to be mentally busy therewith. “To set before one’s face” is also to be understood, in a spiritual sense, as relating to a thing which a man will not put out of his mind. מכשׁול , stumbling-block to sin and guilt (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Eze 7:19</reference>), i.e., the idols. Thus the two phrases simply denote the leaning of the heart and spirit towards false gods. God does not suffer those whose heart is attached to idols to seek and find Him. The interrogative clause 'האדּרשׁ וגו contains a strong negation. The emphasis lies in the infinitive absolute אדּרשׁ et placed before the verb, in which the ה is softened into א, to avoid writing ה twice. נדרשׁ, to allow oneself to be sought, involves the finding of God; hence in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa 65:1</reference> we have נדרשׁ as parallel to נמצא. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">Eze 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:5</reference>, there follows a positive declaration of the attitude of God towards those who are devoted to idolatry in their heart. Every such Israelite will be answered by God according to the measure of the multitude of his idols. The <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> נענה  has not the signification of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, and does not mean “to be answerable,” as Ewald supposes, or to converse; but is generally used in a passive sense, “to be answered,” i.e., to find or obtain a hearing (<reference osisRef="Job.11.2">Job 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>). It is employed here in a reflective sense, to hold or show oneself answering. בה, according to the <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> בהּ, for which the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> suggests the softer gloss בא, refers to 'בּרב גל which follows; the nominative being anticipated, according to an idiom very common in Aramaean, by a previous pronoun. It is written here for the sake of emphasis, to bring the following object into more striking prominence. ב is used here in the sense of <hi type="italic">secundum</hi>, according to, not because, since this meaning is quite unsuitable for the ב in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7">Eze 14:7</reference>, where it occurs in the same connection (בּי). The manner in which God will show Himself answering the idolatry according to their idols, is reserved till Eze 14:8. Here, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:5</reference>, the design of this procedure on the part of God is given: viz., to grasp Israel by the heart; i.e., not merely to touch and to improve them, but to bring down their heart by judgments (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Lev 26:41</reference>), and thus move them to give up idolatry and return to the living God. נזרוּ, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>, to recede, to draw away from God. כּלּם is an emphatic repetition of the subject belonging to נזרוּ.
entries.81eb44b19e22724c334029d49e00d1711271788d: <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6-Ezek.14.8">Eze 14:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14895" type="x-p"/> In these verses the divine threat, and the summons to repent, are repeated, expanded, and uttered in the clearest words. - Eze 14:6. <hi type="italic">Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Repent, and turn away from your idols; and turn away your face from all your abominations. V.7. For every one of the house of Israel, and of the foreigners who sojourn in Israel, if he estrange himself from me, and let his idols rise up in his heart, and set the stumbling-block to his sin before his face, and come to the prophet to seek me for himself; I will show myself to him, answering in my own way.</hi> Eze 14:8. <hi type="italic">I will direct my face against that man, and will destroy him, for a sign and for proverbs, and will cut him off out of my people; and ye shall learn that I am Jehovah.</hi> - לכן in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6">Eze 14:6</reference> is co-ordinate with the לכן in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">Eze 14:4</reference>, so far as the thought is concerned, but it is directly attached to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:5</reference></hi>: because they have estranged themselves from God, therefore God requires them to repent and turn. For God will answer with severe judgments every one who would seek God with idols in his heart, whether he be an Israelite, or a foreigner living in the midst of Israel. שׁוּבוּ, turn, be converted, is rendered still more emphatic by the addition of פניכם... השׁיבוּ. This double call to repentance corresponds to the double reproof of their idolatry in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, viz., שׁוּבוּ, to על לב 'העלה גל; and השׁיבוּ פניכם, to their setting the idols נכח פּניהם. השׁיבוּ is not used intransitively, as it apparently is in <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.30">Eze 18:30</reference>, but is to be taken in connection with the object פניכם, which follows at the end of the verse; and it is simply repeated before פניכם for the sake of clearness and emphasis. The reason for the summons to repent and give up idolatry is explained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7">Eze 14:7</reference>, in the threat that God will destroy every Israelite, and every foreigner in Israel, who draws away from God and attaches himself to idols. The phraseology of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7">Eze 14:7</reference></hi> is adopted almost <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> from <reference osisRef="Lev.17.8">Lev 17:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Lev 17:10</reference>,Lev 17:13. On the obligation of foreigners to avoid idolatry and all moral abominations, vid., <reference osisRef="Lev.20.2">Lev 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.18.26">Lev 18:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Lev 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.19">Exo 12:19</reference>, etc. The ו before ינּזר and יעל does not stand for the <hi type="italic">Vav relat.</hi>, but simply supposes a case: “should he separate himself from my followers, and let his idols rise up, etc.” לדרשׁ־לו בּי does not mean, “to seek counsel of him (the prophet) from me,” for לו cannot be taken as referring to the prophet, although דּרשׁ with ל does sometimes mean to seek any one, and ל may therefore indicate the person to whom one goes to make inquiry (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.13">2Ch 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.4">2Ch 17:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.21">2Ch 31:21</reference>), because it is Jehovah who is sought in this case; and Hävernick’s remark, that “דּרשׁ with ל merely indicates the external object sought by a man, and therefore in this instance the medium or organ through whom God speaks,” is proved to be erroneous by the passages just cited. לו is reflective, or to be taken as a <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>, denoting the inquirer or seeker. The person approached for the purpose of inquiring or seeking, i.e., God, is indicated by the preposition בּ, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:14</reference> (דּרשׁ ); and also frequently, in the case of idols, when either an oracle or help is sought from them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">1Sa 28:7</reference>; 2Ki 1:2.). It is only in this way that לו and בּי can be made to correspond to the same words in the apodosis: Whosoever seeks counsel of God, to him will God show Himself answering בּי, in Him, i.e., in accordance with His nature, in His own way, - namely, in the manner described in Eze 14:8. The threat is composed of passages in the law: 'נתתּי  and 'הכרתּי וגו, after <reference osisRef="Lev.20.3">Lev 20:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.5-Lev.20.6">Lev 20:5-6</reference>; and 'וחשׁמותיהוּ וגו, though somewhat freely, after <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">Deu 28:37</reference> ('היה לשׁמּה למשׁל). There is no doubt, therefore, that השׁמותי is to be derived from שׁמם, and stands for השׁמּותי, in accordance with the custom in later writings of resolving the <hi type="italic">Dagesh forte</hi> into a long vowel. The allusion to <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">Deu 28:37</reference>, compared with היה  in v. 46 of the same chapter, is sufficient to set aside the assumption that השׁמותי is to be derived from שׂים, and pointed accordingly; although the lxx, Targ., Syr., and Vulg. have all renderings of שׂים (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.16">Psa 44:16</reference>). Moreover, שׂים in the perfect never takes the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form; and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> we have אשׁמּם in a similar connection. The expression is a pregnant one: I make him desolate, so that he becomes a sign and proverbs.
entries.e67a1494fc9c346b44824db4c642fb855099cb28: <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9-Ezek.14.11">Eze 14:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen14895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14896" type="x-p"/> No prophet is to give any other answer. - Eze 14:9. <hi type="italic">But if a prophet allow himself to be persuaded, and give a word, I have persuaded this prophet, and will stretch out my hand against him, and cut him off out of my people Israel.</hi> Eze 14:10. <hi type="italic">They shall bear their guilt: as the guilt of the inquirer, so shall the guilt of the prophet be;</hi> Eze 14:11. <hi type="italic">In order that the house of Israel may no more stray from me, and may no more defile itself with all its transgressions; but they may be my people, and I their God is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - The prophet who allows himself to be persuaded is not a prophet מלּבּו (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.2">Eze 13:2</reference>), but one who really thinks that he has a word of God. פּתּה, to persuade, to entice by friendly words (in a good sense, Hos 2:16); but generally <hi type="italic">sensu malo</hi>, to lead astray, or seduce to that which is unallowable or evil. “If he allow himself to be persuaded:” not necessarily “with the hope of payment from the hypocrites who consult him” (Michaelis). This weakens the thought. It might sometimes be done from unselfish good-nature. And “the word” itself need not have been a divine oracle of his own invention, or a false prophecy.
